gloss: The worldwide system of connected computer networks.
examples: I found the recipe on the *internet*.
Our *internet* has been slow since the storm.
She grew up before the *internet* was in every home.

gloss: A set of connected pages on the internet kept by one person or organization.
examples: The company *website* lists all their store hours.
He builds *websites* for small businesses.
You can pay your bill on their *website*.

gloss: A program used to look at pages on the internet.
examples: Try opening the link in a different *browser*.
Most *browsers* will warn you about unsafe sites.
Clear your *browser* history once in a while.

gloss: A word or image you click to go to another place on the internet.
examples: Click the *link* at the bottom of the email.
She sent me three *links* to apartments.
That *link* doesn't work anymore.

gloss: A group of computers or phones connected so they can share information.
examples: The office *network* went down this morning.
Don't log in to your bank on public *networks*.
My phone can't find the *network* out here.

gloss: A wireless connection that lets devices reach the internet.
examples: Does the hotel have free *wifi*?
The *wifi* keeps cutting out in the back bedroom.
I gave my neighbor the *wifi* password.

gloss: A device that connects a home or office to an internet service.
examples: Unplug the *modem* for ten seconds and plug it back in.
The cable company rents *modems* for eight dollars a month.
Our *modem* is older than my car.

gloss: The radio waves that carry a phone call or internet connection.
examples: There's no *signal* in this parking garage.
The *signal* gets weak once you pass the county line.
Cell *signals* are terrible in the mountains.

gloss: A working link between a device and a network.
examples: The video keeps freezing because my *connection* is slow.
We lost our *connection* halfway through the call.
Hotel *connections* are usually too slow for video.

gloss: A file copied from the internet onto your own device.
examples: The *download* took almost an hour.
Check your *downloads* folder for the receipt.
The app has over a million *downloads*.

gloss: A file sent from your device to the internet.
examples: The *upload* failed because the file was too big.
Her latest *upload* got fifty thousand views.
Large *uploads* take forever on this connection.
contrast: The noun is stressed on the first syllable (UP-lohd); the verb is stressed on the second (up-LOHD).

gloss: Unwanted email or messages sent to many people at once.
examples: I get about forty pieces of *spam* a day.
Check your *spam* folder if you don't see our reply.
Most of that *spam* never reaches my inbox.

gloss: A short alert a phone or app shows to tell you something happened.
examples: I turned off *notifications* for that app.
A *notification* popped up during the meeting.
She woke up to sixty *notifications*.

gloss: A program you install on a phone, tablet, or computer.
examples: There's an *app* for tracking your water intake.
I deleted half the *apps* on my phone.
The parking *app* wouldn't take my card.

gloss: The moving mark on a screen that shows where you are pointing or typing.
examples: Put your *cursor* in the first box and start typing.
The *cursor* froze in the middle of the screen.
Both *cursors* showed up when we shared the document.

gloss: One press of a mouse button, or one visit made by clicking a link.
examples: The whole form takes about three *clicks*.
Every *click* on that ad costs the company money.
One more *click* and you're done.

gloss: The first page you see when you open a website.
examples: The sale is right there on the *homepage*.
They redesigned the *homepage* last spring.
Most *homepages* load in under two seconds.

gloss: The name that identifies a website's address on the internet.
examples: He bought the *domain* for twelve dollars a year.
Our *domain* expires next month.
She owns about thirty *domains* she never used.

gloss: A powerful computer that stores files or runs a website for other computers.
examples: The *server* crashed right before the deadline.
All our files sit on a *server* in Virginia.
They're moving the *servers* to a new building.

gloss: Information stored or sent by a computer or phone.
examples: I used up all my *data* watching videos.
The *data* shows a clear drop after March.
They collect *data* on everything you click.
contrast: Historically the plural of Latin datum, but in American English it takes a singular verb: the data is clear.

gloss: An organized store of information kept on a computer.
examples: Your name is already in our *database*.
The library has a *database* of old newspapers.
Two *databases* had the same customer twice.

gloss: A secret set of characters that lets you into an account.
examples: I forgot my *password* again.
Don't use the same *password* on every site.
Good *passwords* are long, not clever.

gloss: The name you use to identify yourself when signing in to an account.
examples: Your *username* is your email address.
That *username* is already taken.
He uses the same *username* everywhere.

gloss: The act of signing in to an account, or the name and password used to do it.
examples: Your *login* should arrive by email tomorrow.
We had three failed *logins* from the same address.
The *login* screen keeps timing out.

gloss: The right to keep your personal information from being seen or shared.
examples: Read the *privacy* policy before you sign up.
People care more about *privacy* than they did ten years ago.
The app's *privacy* settings are buried three menus deep.
contrast: Americans say PRY-vuh-see; the British usually say PRIV-uh-see.

gloss: Protection against theft, damage, or unwanted access.
examples: The bank added another layer of *security*.
Weak passwords are a *security* problem.
*Security* on that site is a joke.

gloss: A system that blocks unwanted traffic from reaching a computer or network.
examples: The *firewall* is blocking that program.
Company *firewalls* usually block streaming sites.
Turn the *firewall* back on when you're done.

gloss: Software written to damage a computer or steal information from it.
examples: That download was full of *malware*.
The scan found *malware* on two machines.
Most *malware* arrives through email attachments.

gloss: Someone who breaks into computer systems without permission.
examples: A *hacker* got into the payroll system.
*Hackers* stole millions of customer records.
The company hired a *hacker* to test its defenses.

gloss: The act of breaking into computer systems without permission.
examples: He got two years in prison for *hacking*.
The report blames *hacking* for the outage.
*Hacking* into a school's grade system is still a crime.

gloss: The trick of sending fake messages to get people to give up passwords or card numbers.
examples: That email is *phishing* — don't click anything.
The bank sent a warning about *phishing*.
Our company runs *phishing* tests twice a year.
contrast: Sounds exactly like fishing; the ph spelling is the only difference.

gloss: The scrambling of information so that only the right person can read it.
examples: The app uses end-to-end *encryption*.
*Encryption* keeps your messages private on public wifi.
Without *encryption*, anyone on the network can read it.

gloss: A store of recently used data that a device keeps so it loads faster next time.
examples: Clear your *cache* and try the page again.
The browser *cache* was holding an old version.
Both *caches* filled up within a day.
contrast: Pronounced like cash, one syllable — not ka-SHAY.

gloss: The amount of data a connection can carry in a given time.
examples: Video calls eat up a lot of *bandwidth*.
We don't have the *bandwidth* for four people streaming.
The plan gives you more *bandwidth* at night.

gloss: A company that sells internet or phone service.
examples: We switched *providers* to save thirty dollars a month.
My internet *provider* raised the price again.
There's only one *provider* in this whole town.

gloss: A company that runs a cellphone network.
examples: Which *carrier* do you use?
The phone is locked to one *carrier*.
All the big *carriers* offer the same plan now.

gloss: A fast, always-on internet connection.
examples: Half the county still has no *broadband*.
*Broadband* runs about sixty dollars a month here.
The school gave out laptops but couldn't give out *broadband*.

gloss: A place or device that gives nearby devices wireless internet.
examples: I turned my phone into a *hotspot*.
The library has a free *hotspot* out front.
There are *hotspots* in most coffee shops downtown.

gloss: The use of a phone on another company's network, usually in another country.
examples: Turn off *roaming* before you land.
*Roaming* charges cost her two hundred dollars.
The plan includes *roaming* in Canada and Mexico.

gloss: The person or address that a message comes from.
examples: Always check the *sender* before you open an attachment.
The *sender* used a fake company name.
You can block *senders* you don't recognize.

gloss: The person a message or package is sent to.
examples: Add the *recipient* before you hit send.
The email went out to two thousand *recipients*.
The *recipient* never picked up the package.

gloss: An online service where people post, share, or sell things.
examples: She posts the same video on three *platforms*.
The *platform* banned his account.
Every *platform* has its own rules about ads.

gloss: The page on a site that holds your name, photo, and information about you.
examples: Her *profile* says she works in Chicago.
I made my *profile* private.
Fake *profiles* are all over that site.

gloss: A small picture or figure that stands for a person online.
examples: His *avatar* is a cartoon dog.
You can change your *avatar* in settings.
Half the *avatars* in the chat were cats.

gloss: Someone who has chosen to see another person's posts.
examples: She has about nine thousand *followers*.
He lost a lot of *followers* after that post.
One *follower* commented on every single photo.

gloss: The running list of posts a site shows you.
examples: My *feed* is nothing but ads lately.
Scroll down your *feed* and you'll see it.
The two *feeds* show completely different news.

gloss: The list of a person's posts shown in the order they were made.
examples: It's still on my *timeline* from last June.
She cleaned up her *timeline* before the job interview.
Their *timelines* are full of vacation photos.

gloss: A photo you take of yourself, usually with a phone.
examples: He took a *selfie* in front of the stadium.
My grandmother sends me *selfies* every Sunday.
One more *selfie* and then we'll go.

gloss: Someone who pays for or signs up to receive a service or channel.
examples: The newsletter has forty thousand *subscribers*.
Only *subscribers* can read the full article.
He gained a thousand *subscribers* in one week.

gloss: A word marked with a # sign that groups posts on the same topic.
examples: The *hashtag* was trending all afternoon.
Don't put twenty *hashtags* on one photo.
Search that *hashtag* and you'll find the whole thread.

gloss: A small picture used in a message to show a feeling or thing.
examples: She answered with a single thumbs-up *emoji*.
My dad uses *emojis* completely wrong.
There's an *emoji* for almost every food.

gloss: Something written or shared on a website for others to see.
examples: Her *post* about the storm got shared everywhere.
He deletes his *posts* after a few days.
That was the first *post* on the whole page.

gloss: A short written response left under a post or article.
examples: Read the *comments* if you want to lose your faith in people.
She left a nice *comment* on my photo.
The paper turned off *comments* on that story.

gloss: An answer sent back to a message or comment.
examples: I sent it Monday and still haven't gotten a *reply*.
His *replies* are always one word long.
Send a quick *reply* so she knows you saw it.

gloss: An exchange of short typed messages online.
examples: The whole family is in one group *chat*.
I muted three *chats* this morning.
There's a live *chat* button on their support page.

gloss: An app for sending messages, or a person who carries messages.
examples: Send me the address on *messenger*.
A bike *messenger* dropped off the contract.
She uses two different *messengers* for work and family.

gloss: A website where someone posts articles or a personal journal.
examples: She writes a food *blog* on the weekends.
I found the fix on somebody's *blog*.
Half those *blogs* haven't been updated in years.

gloss: Someone who writes a blog.
examples: A local *blogger* broke the story first.
The restaurant invited *bloggers* to the opening.
He's been a full-time *blogger* since 2019.

gloss: An audio program you download or stream in episodes.
examples: I listen to a true-crime *podcast* on my commute.
They record the *podcast* in his garage.
There are *podcasts* about absolutely everything now.

gloss: Someone with a large online following who is paid to promote products.
examples: The brand hired an *influencer* to push the new sneaker.
*Influencers* got free rooms for the whole weekend.
She quit teaching to become a fitness *influencer*.

gloss: A joke, image, or video that spreads quickly online.
examples: That *meme* was everywhere last summer.
He explains *memes* to his parents at dinner.
Somebody turned the mayor's speech into a *meme*.
contrast: One syllable, MEEM — not MEH-may or MEM.

gloss: Someone who posts rude things online just to upset people.
examples: Don't feed the *troll*.
The *trolls* found her post within an hour.
One *troll* can ruin a whole comment section.

gloss: A program that acts on its own online, often pretending to be a person.
examples: That account is obviously a *bot*.
*Bots* bought up all the concert tickets.
A *bot* answered before a real person did.

gloss: A program that holds a typed conversation with a person.
examples: The *chatbot* couldn't answer my question.
Most airlines make you fight a *chatbot* first.
They replaced two support agents with *chatbots*.

gloss: A set of steps a computer follows to solve a problem or choose what to show you.
examples: The *algorithm* decides what shows up in your feed.
They changed the *algorithm* and her views dropped.
Nobody outside the company knows how the *algorithms* work.

gloss: A block on a website that makes you pay before you can read more.
examples: The article is behind a *paywall*.
Most big papers put up a *paywall* years ago.
Some *paywalls* let you read three stories a month.

gloss: Headlines written to make people click, not to tell them anything.
examples: That headline is pure *clickbait*.
The site runs on *clickbait* and ads.
I stopped reading anything that looks like *clickbait*.

gloss: A video broadcast over the internet as it happens.
examples: The church puts a *livestream* up every Sunday.
Her *livestream* had four thousand people watching.
They ran two *livestreams* at the same time.

gloss: A chosen list of songs or videos played one after another.
examples: He made a *playlist* for the road trip.
My workout *playlist* is mostly from the nineties.
She has *playlists* for every mood.

gloss: Playing video or music over the internet without downloading it first.
examples: *Streaming* eats through your data fast.
The family pays for four *streaming* services.
*Streaming* killed the DVD business.

gloss: A click that shows you approve of a post.
examples: The photo got two hundred *likes* overnight.
He counts every *like* on every post.
One *like* from her and he was happy all day.

gloss: A person who uses a computer, app, or service.
examples: The app has two million *users*.
Every *user* has to agree to the terms.
New *users* get a free month.

gloss: The part of a program a person sees and uses.
examples: The new *interface* takes some getting used to.
Their *interface* is clean but slow.
Both *interfaces* look the same on a phone.

gloss: A screen that shows the main information and controls in one place.
examples: Log in and you'll land on the *dashboard*.
The *dashboard* shows your usage for the month.
He built two *dashboards* for the sales team.

gloss: A small picture on a screen that stands for a program or command.
examples: Tap the little gear *icon*.
The *icons* on my desktop are a mess.
That *icon* means the file is still uploading.

gloss: A list of choices shown on a screen.
examples: It's under the settings *menu*.
The *menu* on the left has all the sections.
Too many *menus* and people give up.

gloss: One of the choices you can change to control how something works.
examples: Change that *setting* and the noise stops.
All my *settings* got wiped in the update.
There's a *setting* to turn off autoplay.

gloss: One of the choices available to you.
examples: Pick the second *option* on the list.
You have three *options* for shipping.
Canceling isn't really an *option* right now.

gloss: One particular form of something that exists in several forms.
examples: Which *version* of the app are you running?
The free *version* has ads.
There are two *versions* of that story going around.
contrast: Americans say VUR-zhun with a soft zh; the British usually say VUR-shun.

gloss: A small, usually temporary fault in a machine or program.
examples: There's a *glitch* in the checkout page.
A few *glitches* are normal right after launch.
The whole thing was a software *glitch*.

gloss: A mistake, or a message telling you something went wrong.
examples: I keep getting an *error* when I try to save.
The log is full of *errors*.
It was a simple typing *error*.

gloss: A second copy of files kept in case the first is lost.
examples: Luckily I had a *backup* from Tuesday.
The system makes *backups* every night.
No *backup*, no sympathy.

gloss: Space where files are kept on a device or online.
examples: My phone is out of *storage* again.
The free plan gives you five gigabytes of *storage*.
Photos take up most of my *storage*.

gloss: A unit of computer storage equal to about a billion bytes.
examples: The movie is almost four *gigabytes*.
One *gigabyte* doesn't go very far anymore.
My plan comes with ten *gigabytes* a month.

gloss: A unit of computer storage equal to about a million bytes.
examples: The email bounced because the file was over ten *megabytes*.
A photo is usually a few *megabytes*.
One *megabyte* used to feel like a lot.

gloss: A basic unit of computer information, usually eight bits.
examples: One letter of text takes about one *byte*.
The file is a few thousand *bytes*.
Every *byte* counts on a connection this slow.

gloss: One of the tiny dots that make up a picture on a screen.
examples: Zoom in and you can see the *pixels*.
There's a dead *pixel* in the corner of my monitor.
The image is twelve hundred *pixels* wide.

gloss: The amount of detail in a screen or image, measured in pixels.
examples: Send me the photo at a higher *resolution*.
The screen has the same *resolution* as last year's model.
The camera shoots at three different *resolutions*.

gloss: Pictures and designs made or shown by a computer.
examples: The *graphics* in that game are unbelievable.
Our laptop can't handle heavy *graphics*.
She does the *graphics* for the station's weather segment.
contrast: Always ends in -s but takes a singular verb: the graphics is impressive is wrong — say the graphics are impressive.

gloss: A particular style of printed or on-screen letters.
examples: Use a bigger *font* so people in back can read it.
That *font* is hard on the eyes.
The program comes with a hundred *fonts*.

gloss: The way text and pictures are arranged on a page or screen.
examples: The new *layout* is easier to read on a phone.
They tried three *layouts* before picking one.
The *layout* falls apart on a small screen.

gloss: A small piece of software added to a program to give it more features.
examples: Install the *plugin* and the calendar shows up.
Too many *plugins* will slow the site down.
There's a free *plugin* that does exactly that.

gloss: A small add-on for a browser, or an extra number that reaches one phone in an office.
examples: I use an ad-blocking *extension*.
Dial the main number, then *extension* 214.
Disable your *extensions* and see if the page loads.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: The use of scientific knowledge to build machines and tools, or one particular such method.
examples: *Technology* changes faster than the law does.
The hospital invested in new *technology*.
Two competing *technologies* are fighting for the market.

gloss: The main screen of a computer, or a computer meant to sit on a desk.
examples: The file is right there on my *desktop*.
He works on a *desktop* and travels with a tablet.
The office replaced all the old *desktops* last year.

gloss: A small clever device, usually electronic.
examples: He buys every new *gadget* that comes out.
The kitchen is full of *gadgets* nobody uses.
It's a handy little *gadget* for the car.

gloss: A machine that can do work on its own, often controlled by a computer.
examples: A *robot* vacuums their living room every morning.
The plant uses *robots* to weld the frames.
That customer service line sounds like a *robot*.

gloss: A device used to talk to or message people at a distance.
examples: My *phone* died in the middle of the call.
Put your *phones* away during dinner.
She answered the *phone* on the first ring.

gloss: A device for speaking to someone far away over a line or network.
examples: There's a *telephone* on the wall by the register.
The old *telephones* in the building still work.
He wrote down the *telephone* number on a napkin.

gloss: A phone that also runs apps and connects to the internet.
examples: Almost everyone at the meeting had a *smartphone* out.
*Smartphones* replaced cameras for most people.
Her first *smartphone* was a gift from her son.

gloss: A phone that works over a wireless network instead of a wire.
examples: Leave your *cellphone* in the car.
The school collects *cellphones* at the door.
He still uses a flip *cellphone*.
contrast: Americans say cellphone or cell phone; the British say mobile.

gloss: A short written message sent from one phone to another.
examples: Send me a *text* when you land.
I have four unread *texts* from my mom.
His last *text* just said okay.

gloss: A recorded spoken message left for someone who did not answer.
examples: She left a *voicemail* about the appointment.
I have nine *voicemails* I've never listened to.
His *voicemail* is still his ex-wife's voice.

gloss: The sound a phone makes when someone calls.
examples: That's my *ringtone* — sorry.
He set a different *ringtone* for each of his kids.
People used to pay money for *ringtones*.

gloss: A device that makes sound, or a person talking to a group.
examples: Put me on *speaker* so everyone can hear.
One of the *speakers* in the car is blown.
The *speaker* went twenty minutes over.

gloss: A device that picks up sound so it can be recorded or sent.
examples: Your *microphone* is muted.
They set up two *microphones* on the stage.
The *microphone* on this laptop is terrible.

gloss: Earphones with a microphone attached, worn on the head.
examples: He wears a *headset* all day at the call center.
The office ordered thirty new *headsets*.
My *headset* cuts out every few minutes.

gloss: A small camera used for video calls or online video.
examples: Turn your *webcam* on so we can see you.
He covers his *webcam* with tape.
Cheap *webcams* look grainy in low light.

gloss: A person whose phone number or address you have saved.
examples: Add me as a *contact* so I don't go to spam.
I lost all my *contacts* when the phone died.
She has a *contact* at the newspaper.
contrast: The noun is stressed on the first syllable, KAHN-takt; the verb is kun-TAKT.

gloss: The details that say where a person, building, or account can be reached.
examples: What's your email *address*?
The package went to the wrong *address*.
Both *addresses* on the form are old.
contrast: As a noun most Americans stress the first syllable, AD-ress; the verb is always uh-DRESS.

gloss: A list of names, numbers, or files arranged in order.
examples: Her number isn't in the *directory*.
The building *directory* is next to the elevator.
The files are in two different *directories*.

gloss: A person or company that connects or manages phone calls and service.
examples: Press zero to reach an *operator*.
The *operator* put me through to billing.
Three *operators* share the same tower.

gloss: The sending of a signal, message, or program.
examples: The *transmission* cut off in the middle of a word.
They picked up a strange *transmission* on that frequency.
All *transmissions* are recorded.

gloss: How well a radio, TV, or phone picks up a signal.
examples: *Reception* is bad in the basement.
We get better *reception* by the window.
The new antenna improved *reception* a lot.

gloss: The particular rate of radio waves a station or device uses.
examples: The station broadcasts on a low *frequency*.
Emergency crews use their own *frequencies*.
Turn the dial until you find the right *frequency*.

gloss: The crackling noise that spoils a radio or phone signal.
examples: All I could hear was *static*.
There's a lot of *static* on this line.
The storm filled the radio with *static*.

gloss: Unwanted signals that disturb a radio, phone, or wireless connection.
examples: The microwave causes *interference* with the wifi.
There's too much *interference* to hear you.
Power lines can create *interference*.

gloss: How loud a sound is.
examples: Turn the *volume* down, please.
The *volume* on my laptop only goes so high.
He fell asleep with the *volume* all the way up.

gloss: The part of a phone you hold to your ear, or a device that picks up signals.
examples: She picked up the *receiver* and said nothing.
The radio *receiver* needs a new antenna.
Both *receivers* were off the hook.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: The system of sending pictures and sound to be watched, or a set that shows them.
examples: She works in *television*.
They bought a new *television* for the den.
There are three *televisions* in that little apartment.

gloss: A program sent out on radio, television, or the internet.
examples: The *broadcast* starts at seven.
They interrupted the *broadcast* with a weather warning.
Old *broadcasts* are stored in the station's archive.

gloss: A company or channel that sends out radio or television programs.
examples: That *station* plays country all day.
Local *stations* covered the fire live.
He worked at a radio *station* in college.

gloss: Newspapers, television, radio, and websites taken together as a way of reaching the public.
examples: The *media* covered the trial for weeks.
She never talks to the *media*.
Social *media* changed how people get their news.
contrast: Originally the plural of medium; in everyday American English it takes a singular verb: the media is.

gloss: Newspapers and the reporters who work for them.
examples: The *press* was waiting outside the courthouse.
He gave a statement to the *press*.
The story got a lot of bad *press*.

gloss: A printed publication of news that comes out regularly.
examples: He reads the *newspaper* with his coffee.
Two *newspapers* in the state closed last year.
The story made the front page of every *newspaper*.
contrast: Americans say NOOZ; the British say NYOOZ.

gloss: A publication with articles and photos that comes out weekly or monthly.
examples: There were old *magazines* all over the waiting room.
She writes for a travel *magazine*.
The *magazine* stopped printing and went online.

gloss: A piece of writing on one subject in a newspaper, magazine, or website.
examples: Did you read the *article* about the school board?
He's written a dozen *articles* on the topic.
The *article* is behind a paywall.

gloss: The title printed above a news story.
examples: The *headline* was worse than the story.
He only reads the *headlines*.
That trade made *headlines* all over the country.

gloss: Someone who gathers news and writes or broadcasts it.
examples: A *reporter* called the house twice.
*Reporters* crowded around the front steps.
She was a police *reporter* for eleven years.

gloss: A reporter who sends news from a particular place or on a particular subject.
examples: Their White House *correspondent* asked the first question.
The network keeps *correspondents* in a dozen countries.
He spent four years as a war *correspondent*.

gloss: A short regular publication emailed or mailed to a list of people.
examples: Sign up for our weekly *newsletter*.
I unsubscribed from about twenty *newsletters*.
The school sends a *newsletter* home every Friday.

gloss: A printed or online magazine, paper, or book, or the act of putting one out.
examples: The story ran in three different *publications*.
*Publication* was delayed until the spring.
It's a small *publication* with a loyal readership.

gloss: A public notice paid for to sell something or to spread information.
examples: They ran an *advertisement* in the Sunday paper.
The site is buried in *advertisements*.
That *advertisement* has been on the radio for months.
contrast: Americans say ad-vur-TYZE-munt; the British say ud-VUR-tiss-munt.

gloss: A short form of advertisement, used constantly in speech.
examples: I paid extra to skip the *ads*.
She found the apartment through a classified *ad*.
That *ad* plays before every single video.

gloss: An advertisement shown on television or radio.
examples: Everyone watches the game for the *commercials*.
A car *commercial* came on during the news.
He was in a *commercial* for an insurance company.

gloss: A large outdoor board carrying an advertisement.
examples: There's a *billboard* for the casino every ten miles.
The city voted to ban new *billboards*.
His face is on a *billboard* off the interstate.

gloss: A planned series of actions or ads aimed at one goal.
examples: The ad *campaign* cost them millions.
She ran his *campaign* for city council.
Both *campaigns* bought time on local radio.

gloss: A piece of information sent from one person to another.
examples: I left a *message* with his secretary.
She sent three *messages* before I woke up.
The *message* never went through.

gloss: A written message sent to someone, usually by mail.
examples: He wrote her a *letter* every week that summer.
The *letters* were tied with a ribbon in a shoebox.
A *letter* from the IRS is never good news.

gloss: A card with a picture on one side, mailed without an envelope.
examples: She sent a *postcard* from the Grand Canyon.
There's a rack of *postcards* by the register.
The *postcard* arrived after she got home.

gloss: Something wrapped or boxed and sent through the mail.
examples: A *package* is sitting on the porch.
Two *packages* went to the wrong house.
The *package* should get there by Thursday.

gloss: The bringing of mail, packages, or goods to a place.
examples: The *delivery* is running a day late.
They make *deliveries* twice a week.
Free *delivery* on orders over thirty dollars.

gloss: A copy of a document sent over a phone line, or the machine that sends it.
examples: The clinic still wants the form by *fax*.
Two *faxes* came in overnight.
Nobody in the office knows how to work the *fax*.

gloss: A short piece of writing to remind or inform someone.
examples: He left a *note* on the counter.
I take *notes* during every call.
There was a *note* taped to the door.

gloss: A public statement telling people something has happened or will happen.
examples: They made the *announcement* over the intercom.
The morning *announcements* take five minutes.
We're expecting an *announcement* from the mayor today.

gloss: A written or printed statement giving information or a warning.
examples: There's a *notice* posted on the front door.
The bank mailed *notices* to every account holder.
We got a *notice* that rent is going up.

gloss: A talk between two or more people.
examples: We had a long *conversation* about the move.
I overheard two *conversations* about layoffs.
That's a *conversation* for another day.

gloss: Something said, written, or done as an answer or reaction.
examples: Her *response* came within the hour.
We got over five hundred *responses* to the survey.
There's been no *response* from the company.

gloss: A story people pass around that may not be true.
examples: There's a *rumor* that the plant is closing.
*Rumors* spread through the office by lunchtime.
He heard the *rumor* from three different people.

gloss: Someone who listens to a program, podcast, or person.
examples: The show has about a million *listeners*.
A *listener* called in with the answer.
He's a good *listener*, which is rare.

gloss: Someone who watches a program or video.
examples: Ten million *viewers* watched the finale.
One *viewer* wrote in to complain.
The channel is losing younger *viewers*.

gloss: Help given to customers who have trouble with a product or service.
examples: I was on hold with *support* for forty minutes.
Technical *support* is only open on weekdays.
Their customer *support* is the reason I stayed.

gloss: A lesson or guide that shows you step by step how to do something.
examples: I fixed the sink by watching a *tutorial*.
The app opens with a short *tutorial*.
There are hundreds of *tutorials* for that program.

gloss: An attempt to find something, especially by typing words into a website.
examples: A quick *search* turned up her phone number.
The site logs every *search* you make.
Two *searches* gave me completely different results.
